weaknesses: The finite-model theorem contains a fundamental conditioning error. From Equations (9)-(11), the incorrect-model contribution is proportional to E[V(x_k) 1{i_k≠i*}], but the proof effectively replaces this with E[V(x_k)]Pr(i_k≠i*). These quantities cannot be factorized because model selection depends on the same trajectory that determines x_k. Proposition 3.1 only bounds the marginal error probability, so the logarithmic-regret argument does not follow. The same step is reused in the other main theorems.

Assumption 3 is impossible as written for finite b. Equation (7) uniformly bounds the normalized prediction discrepancy, whereas Assumption 3 requires it to exceed d_u c_e σ_u² for every σ_u>0; the right-hand side is unbounded. Assumption 4 has the same issue. Consequently, central results are vacuous under their stated assumptions unless the excitation range is restricted and the analysis is revised.

The key parametric-model normalization argument is false. The claimed lower bound on the posterior denominator is independent of sample size, but even for Ω=[-1,1]^p and s_k(θ)=k||θ||², the normalized integral decays as k^{-p/2}. Moreover, an arbitrary compact Ω need not have positive Lebesgue measure, contain a ball around the minimizer, or have the asserted boundary geometry. Thus the e^p bound and headline O(sqrt(Np)) regret are unsupported.

The infinite-class result overstates its generality. Bounded subsets of a normed space need not have finite packing numbers, and bounded Lipschitz functions on the unbounded state-action domain used here are not generally totally bounded in the supremum norm. The cover is also selected from the observed data, yet fixed-model concentration is applied without a uniform or adaptive-cover argument.

The stated Lipschitz-class corollary is algebraically inconsistent with Theorem 2.2. If log m(ε) scales as ε^{-(d_x+d_u)}, minimizing Nε²+log(m(ε))/ε² gives N^{(d_x+d_u+2)/(d_x+d_u+4)}, not the claimed N^{(d_x+d_u)/(d_x+d_u+2)}; for d_x=d_u=1 this is N^{2/3}, not sqrt(N).

The broad claims about neural networks and transformers are only formal: realizability, uniform persistence of excitation, stable nearby optimal policies, posterior computation, and policy computation are not established for such classes. Proposition F.2 is pointwise in an initial state, controller, and small-noise regime and does not establish the uniform assumptions used by the theorems.

The empirical evidence is inadequate and internally inconsistent. It contains only one synthetic linear-quadratic system, no nonlinear or neural model, limited uncertainty reporting, and no code. Randomly generated finite candidates are not stated to include the true dynamics, despite the realizability assumption. The parametric experiment uses an ε and excitation formula inconsistent with Theorem E.1, invokes b→∞ despite that theorem's finite-b condition, and sometimes compares trajectories generated with different noise realizations. Pseudocode also alternates between x_k,u_k and x_j,u_j in the loss normalization.

weaknesses: The central finite-model regret proof is not sound. In the transition from the conditional decomposition in Eqs. The model-selection event depends on the trajectory and can be strongly correlated with the state magnitude, so this factorization is unjustified. It underpins both the summable multiplicative factor and the claimed regret and stability bounds.

The auxiliary q(x) construction used to apply Lemma C.4 is also invalid under Assumption 1. That assumption only bounds the Bellman residual by γ; it does not ensure a residual q(x) that is simultaneously at most γ and at most the one-step expected cost. Indeed, the footnote's construction can give q(x)=γ when the expected cost is below γ, making the required nonnegative term E[l]-q negative.

The infinite-class result applies fixed-model concentration arguments to a packing seeded by an empirical minimizer and therefore selected from the same trajectory being analyzed. A union bound over its cardinality does not handle this adaptive, data-dependent class; a uniform martingale/empirical-process argument is needed.

The parametric proof is fundamentally flawed. For an arbitrary compact Ω, Lebesgue measure can be zero, a ball around an empirical minimizer need not lie in Ω, and the asserted volume ratio |B_δ|/|Ω|≥δ^p is false. Moreover, the claimed h(δ)=O(δ²) requires unprovided parameter smoothness, an interior stationary minimizer, and control of constants that generally grow with the sample size. Consequently, the e^p normalization bound and O(sqrt(Np)) regret are not established.

The advertised Lipschitz-function specialization is incorrect as stated. Bounded Lipschitz functions on an unbounded state-action domain need not have finite packing numbers in the supremum norm. Even on a bounded domain, if log m(ε) scales as ε^(-d), minimizing the stated bound Nε²+log(m(ε))/ε² gives N^((d+2)/(d+4)), not the claimed N^(d/(d+2)); for d_x=d_u=1 this is N^(2/3), not sqrt(N).

The scope claims substantially exceed the assumptions. Realizability, uniform persistence of excitation over every state and candidate policy, exact certainty-equivalent policies, and strong global Bellman inequalities are restrictive. The parameter-identifiability assumption is especially incompatible with the permutation and scaling symmetries of ordinary neural networks and transformers, despite these being highlighted as canonical applications.

The experiments do not validate the nonlinear or large-model claims: they use only one linear-quadratic system, contain no competitive baselines, mostly report individual trajectories without uncertainty, and sometimes compare controllers under different noise realizations. Algorithm 3 exhibits roughly two orders of magnitude state overshoot, contradicting the characterization of benign transients.

The finite-model experiment is internally inconsistent with realizability. As written, every candidate is sampled continuously at random, so the true model is almost surely absent, yet the theory requires f∈F and the displayed parameter error reaches zero. Other essential details—including process-noise variance, b, seeds, code, and treatment of unstabilizable sampled models—are missing; thus the theorem's learning-rate condition cannot be checked.

Several implementation claims are inaccurate or incomplete: the theoretical exploration schedule depends on unknown separation constants despite a claim otherwise, the reported finite-bank complexities omit important factors of m and dense matrix costs, and high-dimensional truncated-Gaussian rejection sampling can be exponentially inefficient. These issues further weaken reproducibility and practical significance.

Setting S2 incorrectly treats boundedness as sufficient for a finite packing or cover. Bounded subsets of infinite-dimensional normed spaces need not be totally bounded, and Algorithm 4 may never terminate. In particular, the claimed metric-entropy example for bounded Lipschitz functions is not valid on the manuscript's unbounded state-action domain without additional compact-domain assumptions.

The persistence, Bellman-stability, and policy-continuity assumptions are extremely strong and are not verified for the broad nonlinear, neural-network, or transformer classes highlighted in the abstract. Much of the exploration and stability difficulty is effectively placed inside these assumptions, making comparisons with general RL guarantees and claims of optimality insufficiently supported.

The empirical evidence is inadequate for the practical claims: there are no competing learning baselines, uncertainty estimates are mostly absent, and comparisons to the optimal controller sometimes use different noise realizations. The stated linear S1 construction does not explain how the true model is included despite random continuous sampling, while the S3 experimental exploration schedule differs from Theorem E.1. Reproducibility details such as noise levels, initialization, and code are missing.

Claims of benign transients are contradicted by the parametric experiment, where the state norm grows by roughly two orders of magnitude above the comparator. The paper also understates the difficulty of sampling a high-dimensional truncated posterior and computing a new nonlinear policy at each update.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: non-episodic learning and control with continuous states, actions, and potentially nonlinear dynamics.
The combination of exponential-weight model selection, explicit excitation, and certainty-equivalent control is intuitive, and the finite-model identification argument may be a useful starting point.

The linear-control and nonlinear pendulum examples illustrate how the proposed approach could be coupled with LQR and model-predictive control, including a finite-model experiment with up to 10,000 candidates.
weaknesses: The main regret proof contains a fundamental dependence error. In passing from equations (9)-(11) to the recurrence underlying equation (6), the analysis effectively replaces E[V(x_k)1{i_k≠i*}] by E[V(x_k)]Pr(i_k≠i*). These quantities cannot be factorized: i_k is sampled from trajectory-dependent scores and is generally correlated with x_k. A marginal O(k^-2) model-selection error probability does not control the state magnitude on the error event, especially when a wrong controller may destabilize the system. This invalidates Theorem 3.2 and propagates to Theorems D.2 and E.1.

A second key step in the same proof is unsupported. Assumption 1 only upper-bounds the Bellman residual by γ, but the proposed construction of q(x) does not ensure both q(x)≤γ and q(x)≤E[l(x,u)], as required to make the negative term in Lemma C.4 nonnegative. Under an average-cost Bellman equality, the residual equals γ and immediately violates the claimed property at states whose instantaneous expected cost is below γ.

The parametric-model theorem has major measure and regularity gaps. A compact set Ω contained in a unit ball may have zero Lebesgue measure, and a ball centered at a minimizer need not lie inside Ω. No assumption guarantees smoothness in θ, an interior minimizer, or the claimed h(δ)=O(δ²) behavior. Moreover, the hidden curvature can grow with the number of accumulated samples. Consequently, the denominator lower bound used in Appendix E and the resulting O(sqrt(d_u N p)) guarantee are not established.

The advertised applicability to neural networks and transformers is particularly unconvincing: Assumption 6 requires global quadratic identifiability in Euclidean parameter distance, whereas standard neural architectures have permutation, scaling, and other parameter symmetries that give different parameters representing the same function.

The nonparametric claim is overstated. A bounded subset of an infinite-dimensional normed space need not have finite packing numbers. In particular, bounded Lipschitz functions on the unbounded domain R^(d_x+d_u) are not totally bounded in the supremum norm, so the asserted metric-entropy rate and no-regret example require an unstated compact-domain assumption. Assumption 4 is also implausible for this class because functions may differ in remote regions that a finite trajectory visits with arbitrarily small probability.

Several stability claims have additional gaps. Corollary C.5 infers a lower bound on l in terms of V without accounting for the additive and linear terms permitted by smoothness, and a uniform second-moment bound does not by itself imply the asserted uniform sub-Gaussian control. The b→∞ analysis likewise does not repair the central state/error-event dependence problem.

The empirical evaluation is insufficient for the breadth of the claims: it has no competing learning baselines, very limited multi-seed statistics, and only two simulated systems. Important reproducibility details such as process-noise levels, normalization b, seeds, and code are missing. The finite-model experiment does not clearly state that the exact true model was inserted despite continuous random candidate generation, and the nonlinear misspecification assumptions are not verified. The parametric experiment uses b→∞ even though the stated Theorem E.1 condition degenerates in that limit.

Practicality is overstated. The S2 procedure requires generally intractable optimization, covering, and policy computation; general S3 sampling and policy optimization are also intractable without approximation or mixing guarantees. The paper additionally gives inconsistent O(p²) versus effectively O(p) sampling-complexity statements and repeatedly labels the Algorithm 3 experiment as setting S2 rather than S3.
